questions.q: In cache-aside (lazy loading), what happens on a cache miss?
options: The cache itself fetches the value from the database
The request fails and the client retries later
A background job repopulates the whole cache from the database on a schedule
The application reads the database, then stores the value in the cache
questions.explanation: In cache-aside the application owns the miss path: it queries the database and writes the result back into the cache. A read-through cache is what fetches on the app's behalf.

questions.q: In write-through caching, a write is acknowledged when?
options: It reaches the backing store, bypassing the cache entirely on the way
After both the cache and the backing store are updated
Once the cache holds it, with the store updated later
After the entire cache is invalidated
questions.explanation: Write-through updates cache and store synchronously before acknowledging, keeping them consistent at the cost of write latency. Acknowledging from the cache alone is write-back.

questions.q: Which eviction policy removes the entry that has gone unused for the longest time?
options: FIFO (first-in, first-out)
LFU (least frequently used)
LRU (least recently used)
Random replacement
questions.explanation: LRU evicts by recency of access, betting that recently used items will be used again. FIFO evicts by insertion order and LFU by access count, both ignoring recency.

questions.q: What is the main risk of write-back (write-behind) caching?
options: Losing acknowledged writes if the cache fails before flushing
Consistently higher write latency than write-through caching on every operation
Every subsequent read becoming a cache miss
Duplicate keys accumulating inside the cache
questions.explanation: Write-back acknowledges before the backing store is updated, so a crash loses whatever has not yet flushed. Its latency is lower than write-through, which is exactly why it takes this risk.

questions.q: What does setting a TTL on a cache entry accomplish?
options: It tracks how many times each key was hit for eviction decisions
It bounds staleness by expiring the entry after a set time
It encrypts the value at rest
It reserves memory ahead of future writes
questions.explanation: A TTL guarantees an entry is refetched after a known interval, capping how stale the served data can be. It is the simplest form of invalidation.

questions.q: A CDN primarily caches what, and where?
options: Database rows, colocated inside the application tier
User sessions, stored only in the browser
Static or cacheable content, at edge locations near users
Write buffers, held durably in regional data centers close to origins
questions.explanation: CDNs replicate static or publicly cacheable assets to edge PoPs close to users, cutting round-trip latency and origin load. They are a read-path optimization, not a write buffer.

questions.q: A cache serves 900 of 1,000 reads without touching the database. What is the hit ratio?
questions.explanation: Hit ratio is hits divided by total requests: 900/1000 is 90%. The remaining 10% is the miss ratio that reaches the database.

questions.q: Which data is the best fit for aggressive caching?
options: Bank account balances during active transfers
A user's unread-message counter
Shopping cart contents during checkout
Product catalog pages read by millions
questions.explanation: Catalog pages are read far more often than written and tolerate brief staleness, the ideal caching profile. Balances, counters, and carts change frequently and demand fresh reads.

questions.q: A hot key expires and 10,000 concurrent requests all miss and hit the database at once. Name and fix?
options: Cache poisoning; fixed by checksumming values
Cache eviction pressure; fixed by adding much more RAM to the cluster
A cache stampede; mitigated with locks, request coalescing, or staggered TTLs
A hot partition; fixed by resharding the database tier
questions.explanation: This is a cache stampede, and the fix is to let one request rebuild the key while others wait or serve stale, plus jittered TTLs. More RAM does not help since the key expired rather than being evicted.

questions.q: You update a database row while the cache still holds the old value with 10 minutes of TTL left. Best practice?
options: Invalidate or update the cache entry as part of the write path
Simply wait for the TTL to expire naturally, since caches are best-effort
Restart the cache cluster to clear stale entries
Shorten every TTL globally to one second
questions.explanation: Explicit invalidation on write closes the staleness window immediately for just the affected key. Waiting out the TTL serves wrong data, and one-second TTLs everywhere destroys the hit ratio.

questions.q: Why can CDN caching break personalized pages?
options: CDNs cannot serve HTTPS content at the edge
Personalized pages are too small to be worth caching
Edge servers strip session cookies from every response they forward downstream
One user's cached response may be served to other users
questions.explanation: A shared edge cache keyed only by URL will hand one user's personalized HTML to the next visitor, a real data-leak class of bug. Mark such responses private or vary the cache key.

questions.q: Cache-aside: server A updates the DB then deletes the key; server B read the old DB value just before. What can happen?
options: A deadlock between the two servers
B repopulates the cache with the stale value after A's delete
The key gets deleted twice and corrupts the cache
The database rejects A's write because of B's concurrently held read lock
questions.explanation: B's in-flight read holds the pre-update value and can write it back after A's delete, leaving stale data cached indefinitely. Delayed double-delete or versioned writes mitigate this race.

questions.q: Repeated lookups for nonexistent users keep hammering your database. A standard fix?
options: Cache the 'not found' result briefly (negative caching)
Add an index on every column of the users table
Retry the lookups with exponential backoff
Route the lookups to a read replica
questions.explanation: Storing a short-lived tombstone for missing keys absorbs the repeats at the cache layer. A Bloom filter is the complementary defense against this cache-penetration pattern.

questions.q: Compared with an in-process per-instance cache, a shared cache like Redis offers?
options: Lower access latency than local memory
Zero network overhead for hot keys
Automatic, guaranteed consistency with the backing database on every write
A consistent view across app instances at the cost of a network hop
questions.explanation: One shared copy means every instance sees the same entries and one invalidation suffices, but each access pays a network round trip. Local memory is always faster; it just diverges per instance.

questions.q: Every entry was cached at deploy time with the same one-hour TTL. What happens an hour later?
options: Nothing; caches automatically stagger expirations
Synchronized mass expiry hammers the origin; add jitter to TTLs
The cache compacts itself in the background and no action is needed
Entries refresh silently in the background by default
questions.explanation: Identical TTLs set at the same moment expire together, producing a thundering herd against the origin. Randomizing TTLs by some percentage spreads the refreshes out.

questions.q: A read-heavy service has a 95% hit ratio and its database tops out at 500 QPS. Sustainable total read QPS?
options: About 5,000
About 525
About 10,000
About 100,000
questions.explanation: Only the 5% miss traffic reaches the database, so 500 QPS of misses corresponds to 500/0.05, about 10,000 total reads per second.

questions.q: An LFU cache keeps serving last week's viral story while today's rising story keeps missing. Root cause?
options: LFU evicts the most frequently used entries first
Accumulated frequency counts let old popular items crowd out newcomers
LFU degenerates into LRU under skewed workloads
TTL expiry is fundamentally incompatible with maintaining LFU frequency counters
questions.explanation: Plain LFU never forgets, so a once-viral item's huge count keeps it resident while fresh items are evicted before building up counts. Aging or windowed counters, as in W-TinyLFU, fix this.

questions.q: Sessions live in one Redis node with persistence disabled; it restarts and users are logged out. What would have prevented this?
options: Longer TTLs on all session keys
Switching the eviction policy from LFU to LRU on the node
Replication with failover, or a durable store behind the cache
Raising maxmemory on the node
questions.explanation: The loss came from a single non-durable node, so replicas with failover or a durable backing store is the real fix. TTLs, memory limits, and eviction policy are irrelevant once the process restarts empty.

questions.q: Why is 'cache everything with long TTLs' wrong for a read-mostly system with occasional critical updates?
options: Staleness windows on critical data can break correctness, and invalidation is genuinely hard
Cache memory costs grow without any upper bound over time
Cached reads end up slower than direct database reads
Redis and Memcached cap TTLs at sixty seconds
questions.explanation: A long TTL means a critical update stays invisible for that whole window, and reliably invalidating every derived entry is notoriously difficult. TTLs should match each data type's tolerance for staleness.

questions.q: A cache holds 1M entries; 10M distinct keys are requested uniformly at random. Expected steady-state hit ratio?
options: About 90% in steady state
About 50% in steady state
Nearly 100% once the cache warms up
About 10% in steady state
questions.explanation: With a uniform key distribution the hit ratio is just cache size over key space, 1M/10M, about 10%. Caching only pays off when access is skewed, not uniform.
